questions.title: Does 'pingpong scheduling' imply that we lose half the throughput because warps alternate between doing nothing and working?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the 'pingpong scheduling' concept described in Section 3.1. The text says Warpgroup 1 does softmax while Warpgroup 2 does GEMM, and then they swap roles. My confusion is: during the phase where Warpgroup 1 is doing softmax, isn't Warpgroup 2 effectively idle regarding its *own* softmax task? And vice versa? If the goal is to maximize utilization, doesn't alternating roles mean we are serializing the work of two groups rather than running them fully in parallel? How exactly does this result in a net gain if one group is always waiting for the other to finish its 'slow' part?

questions.title: How can asynchronous WGMMA instructions depend on previous results if they don't wait?
questions.question_body: In Algorithm 2 (FlashAttention-3 consumer warpgroup forward pass), line 14 states 'Compute S_next... Commit but do not wait,' followed later by 'Wait for the WGMMA.' I understand that WGMMA is asynchronous on Hopper. However, line 19 ('Compute m_i... based on S_next') logically requires S_next to be finished. If we commit without waiting at line 14, how does the hardware ensure that the subsequent operations (like calculating max or exp) don't read garbage data from registers before the matrix multiplication completes? Is there an implicit barrier inserted by the compiler that I'm missing, or does the 'Wait' at line 18 strictly enforce this dependency?

questions.title: Why does FP8 WGMMA require k-major layout while FP16 accepts both mn-major and k-major?
questions.question_body: Section 2.2 mentions that for FP8 WGMMA, only k-major format is supported for operands in shared memory, whereas FP16 accepts both. The paper then discusses needing to transpose V tiles in-kernel to satisfy this. Can someone explain *why* this restriction exists specifically for FP8? Is it a limitation of how the Tensor Cores pack the 8-bit data internally versus how they handle 16-bit data? Also, if Q and K are usually stored in a way that makes Q*K^T efficient (likely mn-major or similar depending on storage), why doesn't this same constraint cause issues for the first GEMM ($\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top$) which produces P?

questions.title: If multiplying by an orthogonal matrix M preserves QK^T mathematically, why does it reduce quantization error?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces 'incoherent processing' where we multiply Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix M before quantizing to FP8. Mathematically, $(QM)(KM)^T = QKK^TM^T = QK^T$, so the exact attention score shouldn't change. However, I'm struggling to grasp *how* this helps with quantization error specifically caused by outliers. If M just rotates the vectors, wouldn't the magnitudes of individual elements remain roughly similar (just mixed)? Why does spreading out outliers via rotation make them easier to represent with only 3 bits of mantissa in FP8 compared to leaving them concentrated? Does this rely on statistical properties of Gaussian distributions that aren't immediately obvious?

questions.title: What determines the optimal number of stages 's' in the circular SMEM buffer versus pipeline depth?
questions.question_body: The paper describes using a circular SMEM buffer with $s$ stages for producer-consumer synchronization (Algorithm 1) and also proposes a separate '2-stage' or '3-stage' pipelining scheme for overlapping GEMM and softmax (Algorithm 2). Are these two counts ($s$ stages vs. pipeline depth) coupled? For instance, if I increase $s$ to hide more latency from TMA loads, does that negatively impact my ability to run a deeper GEMM-softmax pipeline due to register pressure or resource contention? The paper mentions register pressure as a limiting factor for extending beyond 2 stages; is there a general rule of thumb derived from their experiments on how many stages one should aim for given a specific block size ($B_r \times B_c$)?

questions.title: Confusion about register permutation: How do byte permute instructions align with logical column permutations?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3 regarding FP8 layout transformations, the authors mention changing the order of entries in registers using byte permute instructions: '$\{ d0 d1 d4 d5 d2 d3 d6 d7 \}$'. They claim this permutes columns of the logical P tile (e.g., columns $0189$ become first four). I am confused about how manipulating bytes within registers translates to permuting columns of a matrix tile held across multiple threads. Since WGMMA distributes matrix rows/columns across threads in a specific pattern defined by PTX architecture rules, how do these specific byte swaps map exactly to moving entire columns without breaking the internal tiling assumptions required by subsequent WGMMA calls?
